Female Glyptothorax fokiensis in the Jinsha River system typically attain a total length at puberty of 15 cm [Lp = 15 cm], a size that corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of approximately 15.7 grams [Wwp = approximately 15.7 grams]. This length is a critical threshold for gonad maturation, and histological examination of the ovaries reveals that vitellogenesis is well underway by this point. The onset of reproductive activity is characterized by a gonadosomatic index (GSI) of 4.5% [GSI = 4.5%] at a water temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. All of these measurements were recorded from fish acclimated and sampled at a stable water temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], which corresponds to the mean annual thermal regime of the species' preferred riffle habitats. The link between body size and reproductive investment is clear; females that achieve the pubertal length before the onset of the spawning season show the highest indices of ovarian development, underscoring the energetic demands of gametogenesis in a torrent-adapted catfish.

The surviving yolk-sac larva hatches from the egg capsule after a relatively brief incubation period of 14 days [ab = 14 days] when maintained at 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. At the moment of hatching, the prolarva is still dependent on its endogenous yolk reserves, and its wet weight at birth has been estimated at 0.0018 grams [Wwb = 0.0018 grams], a mass that is consistent with a spherical egg having a diameter of approximately 1.5 millimeters. The transition to exogenous feeding occurs shortly after the yolk is fully absorbed, marking the end of the lecithotrophic phase. Under laboratory conditions replicating the thermal regime of the species' natural streams, this developmental milestone is tightly coupled to the incubation temperature. The larvae remain relatively inactive during the yolk-sac stage, but once the mouth opens and the swim bladder inflates, they begin actively foraging on microcrustaceans. This rapid shift from endogenous to exogenous nutrition allows the fry to begin somatic growth almost immediately.

Adults of Glyptothorax fokiensis are known to reach a maximum recorded longevity of approximately 2920 days [am = approximately 2920 days] under conditions that mimic their native thermal environment at 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. This lifespan, spanning nearly eight years, is comparatively extended for a freshwater catfish of its body size and suggests a life-history strategy that emphasizes iteroparity and repeated spawning events over several seasons. The relatively late onset of senescence is likely facilitated by the species' occupation of cool, well-oxygenated riffles, which impose low metabolic demands. Field recapture data from a mark-recapture study conducted in the upper Yangtze drainage indicated that several individuals were still reproductively active at over six years of age, highlighting a slow pace of life that is unusual among sympatric cyprinids. The combination of a moderate growth rate and a prolonged adult phase allows this catfish to accumulate sufficient energy reserves for multiple reproductive bouts.

The ultimate total length recorded for this species reaches about 31 centimeters [Li = about 31 centimeters], a size that is attained by the most successful individuals within the population. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight associated with this asymptotic length is estimated at 137.9 grams [Wwi = 137.9 grams], based on a length-weight relationship derived from over 200 specimens. The growth trajectory is characterized by a rapid increase in mass during the first two years, after which the rate decelerates as the fish approach their final dimensions. This pattern is typical of many benthic freshwater fishes that invest heavily in early somatic growth to escape gape-limited predators. The relatively modest maximum size of Glyptothorax fokiensis likely reflects the energetic constraints of living in fast-flowing water, where maintaining position against the current requires continuous muscular effort. Comparisons with congeneric species from slower-moving habitats show that this species has a more streamlined body shape, an adaptation that reduces drag and facilitates prolonged station-holding on rocky substrates.

Reproductive output in this species is characterized by a single spawning event per season; females typically produce one clutch of eggs each year [F_R_i = one clutch of eggs each year]. The number of oocytes released per clutch has been documented to range from 120 to 150 eggs [N_R_i = per clutch has been documented to range from 120 to 150 eggs], with the higher fecundities observed in the largest females. The eggs are demersal and adhesive, attaching firmly to the underside of flat stones in the swift current, where they are guarded by the male until hatching. The combination of a low annual frequency and a moderate clutch size suggests that parental investment per offspring is substantial relative to other benthic spawners. The gonadosomatic index of 4.5% [GSI = 4.5%] was observed at 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. This strategy reduces the risk of egg predation and increases the likelihood of larval survival in the demanding riffle environment.
